name: Flexitarian diet

card.summary: A mostly plant-based diet that allows occasional meat, used by people aiming for lean body composition, clear skin and a sustainable eating pattern.
card.note: Poorly planned versions of low-meat diets may lack some nutrients.

quick.overview:
The flexitarian diet centres on plants, such as vegetables, fruit, legumes and whole grains, while allowing meat and other animal foods in smaller amounts or on some days. It is a flexible middle path between omnivorous and vegetarian eating.

For appearance, people use it as a way to manage weight and body fat with a higher-fibre, lower-calorie pattern while keeping enough protein to train. Reviews describe observational links between reduced red meat and lower diabetes and heart-disease risk; the definition of "flexitarian" varies a lot across studies.
quick.how: Practitioners build meals around plant foods and add smaller portions of meat, fish, eggs or dairy on chosen days, with meat-free days or weeks being a common structure. Athletes and lifters adapting it focus on plant protein sources and meeting protein needs.
quick.risks: Well-planned versions can meet nutrition recommendations, while poorly planned ones may cause deficiencies, reviewers say. Researchers have also discussed whether restrictive eating motives overlap with weight-control behaviours in some people.

lead: The flexitarian diet, also called semi-vegetarian, is a plant-centred eating pattern that allows limited meat and other animal products. Definitions vary by country and study; a Dutch group, for example, counts anyone who skips meat, fish and cold cuts for at least one day a week.[1]

People adopt it for weight management, general health and, in some cases, a leaner physique and better-looking skin through diet quality. The appearance chain runs from more vegetables, legumes and whole grains to higher fibre and lower calorie density, then easier weight control and a leaner look, while some animal foods keep protein intake high enough for training.[2][12] Research summaries link reduced red-meat intake with lower risks of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, though much of this is observational.[1][2] A 2018 review asked whether flexitarian eating helps weight control or can mask restrictive eating.[3]

Dietitian Dawn Jackson Blatner popularised the word through a book; sources date it between 2008 and 2010, and she is described as having coined the term, though the word itself was voted most useful of 2003.[1][12][13] Appearance-focused communities discuss it mostly as one option within wider plant-based and omnivore debates, as in long T Nation threads on vegetarian bodybuilding.[18]

chain: More vegetables, legumes and whole grains
Higher fibre and lower calorie density with adequate protein
Easier weight control and a leaner look
angle.text: People use flexitarian eating to keep body fat down while still getting protein from some animal sources and plant proteins. Athletes use plant-forward patterns while meeting protein needs.

paras: The pattern emphasises fruit, vegetables, legumes and whole grains and reduces meat rather than eliminating it; related terms include demi-vegetarianism, reducetarianism and semi-veganism.[1] Wikipedia reports that the word gained wide use in the 2010s, entered Merriam-Webster's Collegiate Dictionary in 2012 and was voted most useful word of 2003 by the American Dialect Society.[1]

No official definition exists. Studies usually define it as eating less red meat and poultry, and some researchers reserve semi-vegetarian for people who avoid red meat and flexitarian for people who eat very little meat.[1][12] Dutch organisations use different thresholds, one counting a day a week without meat, fish and cold cuts and another counting three or more meat-free days a week.[1]

Self-identification is common and loose: in the Netherlands, flexitarian identification rose from 14% in 2011 to 43% in 2019 while those people reported eating meat on more days per week, leading researchers to suspect the label had grown elastic.[1] Other surveys cited by Wikipedia put the UK meat-free share at 12% in 2018 and a global flexitarian share at about 14%.[1] A 2022 survey of over 12,000 consumers in ten countries, reported by VegNews, found about one in four identify as flexitarian.[13]

The practice of occasional meat eating within a mostly vegetarian pattern is older than the word. Registered dietitian Dawn Jackson Blatner is credited with popularising flexitarian by combining flexible and vegetarian in a book; VegNews says she coined it in 2008, while Today's Dietitian dates her book to 2010.[12][13] She describes the approach as adding plant foods without excluding food groups, and a sample plate is about half colourful produce, a quarter grains and a quarter protein from animal and plant sources.[12]

The word spread into dictionaries and supermarkets. Plant-based meat brands target flexitarian consumers, and a 2019 audit of products on supermarket shelves examined the nutritional profile of plant-based meat substitutes marketed to them.[13][15] On sustainability, global modelling published in 2018 compared diet strategies for health and environmental outcomes, and Wikipedia notes that flexitarian diets give smaller environmental gains than fully plant-based diets but are considered more achievable, with most evidence from modelling.[1][14]

Online, the term appears in fitness forums as one of several options. A 2010 T Nation thread on vegetarian bodybuilding quoted a 2009 Precision Nutrition article on omnivore, vegetarian and flexitarian eating, and a 2021 T Nation thread asks whether vegetables are necessary at all.[18][19] A 2019 Hacker News submission carried the headline 'A bit of meat, a lot of veg', about a flexitarian diet to feed ten billion people.[20]

sections.h: How people use it for their looks
paras: Practitioners build meals around plant foods and add smaller portions of meat, fish, eggs or dairy on chosen days, with meat-free days or weeks a common structure.[12] A sample plan from Today's Dietitian lists planned weekly ranges of meat, fish, pulses, soy, nuts and seeds, and swaps such as mixing mushrooms or beans into ground meat.[12] The stated appearance aims are weight and body-fat control through a higher-fibre, lower-saturated-fat pattern, and clear, healthy-looking skin through produce intake.[12]

Athletes and lifters adapting it focus on plant protein sources and meeting protein needs; a 2020 review of sustainable diets for athletes names meeting, not exceeding, protein requirements through flexitarian and plant-based approaches as one option and calls for more research on training adaptation and recovery.[6]

A 2016 review by Emma Derbyshire in Frontiers in Nutrition identified 25 studies published from 2000 to 2016 on flexitarian diets, twelve of them on body weight and diet quality; it reported emerging evidence suggestive of benefits for body weight, metabolic health markers, blood pressure and type 2 diabetes risk, and noted that women were more likely to be flexitarian while men were more likely to overconsume meat.[2] Today's Dietitian cites a 2015 study in postmenopausal Korean women in which a flexitarian pattern was associated with lower glucose, insulin, insulin resistance, body weight and body fat than a non-vegetarian pattern.[12]

A review of plant-based diet definitions describes where flexitarian patterns sit among vegetarian and vegan diets.[4][5] Reviewers also note that plant-based meat alternatives differ nutritionally from traditional plant foods.[8][15] A 2025 review in Maturitas examines vegetarian diets and longevity.[17] The studies loaded for this article measured weight, metabolic markers, nutrient status and adherence rather than skin or facial appearance.

A 12-week randomised trial of 136 healthy adults aged 20 to 69 compared diets with 70%, 50% and 30% of protein from animal sources. Vitamin B12 intake and status were lower in the mostly-plant group than in the mostly-animal group, iodine was lower in both plant-heavier groups, and iron and folate intakes were higher in the plant group although iron and folate blood markers did not differ; the authors stressed monitoring micronutrients on flexitarian diets.[7]

A 10-week trial of 80 healthy young adults compared a flexitarian diet including red meat with a vegetarian diet including plant-based meat alternatives; adherence averaged 91.5 out of 100, higher in the flexitarian group (96.1 versus 86.7), and both groups increased vegetable intake and reported more positive eating experiences.[9] Prescribing vegetarian or flexitarian diets has been reported to lead to a sustained reduction in meat intake.[10]

The 2018 review by Catherine Forestell notes that carefully planned vegetarian diets can meet nutrition recommendations, that vegetarians show higher rates of disordered and restrained eating than non-vegetarians, and that flexitarians and semi-vegetarians differ in motives from vegans and lacto-ovo vegetarians; the review also cautions that vegetarians are a heterogeneous group.[3] A 2012 study examined the relationship between restrained eating and vegetarianism in college women.[16]

Controlled trials exist on plant-protein substitution and adherence: a 12-week randomized trial of replacing animal proteins with plant proteins,[7] a 10-week randomized flexitarian-versus-vegetarian trial,[9] and randomized crossover studies of plant protein and metabolic markers.[11] Wikipedia notes that most flexitarian evidence is observational, and that environmental benefits come largely from modelling.[1]

lore.intro: Flexitarian eating is discussed in fitness and appearance forums as a flexible alternative to strict vegetarian or omnivore diets, with debate about protein, nutrients and whether the label is meaningful [18][19].

claims.claim: Eating mostly plants keeps body fat down
claims.believers: Dietitians quoted by Today's Dietitian say clients often lose weight without calorie counting while eating more fibre and less saturated fat [12].
claims.experts: Derbyshire's 2016 review reported emerging evidence suggestive of benefits for body weight, with most evidence observational [2][1].

claims.claim: It gives enough protein to build muscle
claims.believers: Lifters on T Nation discuss vegetarian and flexitarian bodybuilding as workable with attention to protein [18].
claims.experts: The 2020 athlete review recommends meeting protein requirements through flexitarian approaches and calls for research on training adaptation [6].

claims.claim: A few meat-free days are enough to be flexitarian
claims.believers: Dutch organisations count one meat-free day a week [1].
claims.experts: Dutch self-identified flexitarians rose from 14% to 43% while eating meat on more days, suggesting the label is loose [1].

claims.claim: It is easy to stick to
claims.believers: Meat-inclusive flexitarian participants in a 2023 trial reported high satisfaction [9].
claims.experts: Adherence averaged 96.1 out of 100 in the flexitarian arm versus 86.7 in the vegetarian arm [9].

claims.claim: Swapping animal for plant protein changes nutrient intake
claims.believers: Plant-forward advocates say it adds fibre, folate and potassium [12].
claims.experts: A 12-week trial found lower B12 and iodine intake and status in plant-heavier arms [7].

claims.believers: Writers on flexitarian eating describe better skin through produce intake [12].
claims.experts: The trials reviewed measure weight, metabolic markers and nutrients, not skin appearance [2][7][9].
